properties.name: Tyre
properties.one_line: Tyre's dye works crushed roughly 10,000 murex shells to yield a single gram of true purple. Workers cracked open each snail by hand and left the glands to ferment in vats along the shore for days. The stench was so strong that Roman law banned dye works from town centers. Excavators in 1909 uncovered mounds of blackened, broken shell outside the city, waste from a trade that had run for over a thousand years.
properties.image_credit: Roman Hippodrome, Tyre, Lebanon, by Vyacheslav Argenberg · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman ruins at Tyre, Lebanon

properties.name: Sidon
properties.one_line: Sidon manufactured purple dye before Tyre ever took the credit for it. Its garbage dump grew into an entire hill of crushed murex shell, a rise still called Murex Hill south of the old castle. Between 10,000 and 20,000 snails went into a single gram of dye, making a robe worth more than a house. Greeks called the Phoenicians who ran this trade the 'purple people.'
properties.image_credit: Sidon Sea Castle · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Sea Castle at Sidon, Lebanon

properties.name: Meninx
properties.one_line: Meninx turned the island of Djerba into North Africa's biggest purple-dye metropolis. Pliny the Elder and Strabo both singled the town out for its wealth from murex trunculus shell. Unlike other dye sites, Meninx dyed the cloth itself on-site rather than shipping raw dye elsewhere. Geophysical surveys since 2015 have traced its baths, theater, and warehouses beneath the sand.
properties.image_credit: Archaeological Site, Meninx · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ruins at the Meninx archaeological site, Djerba

properties.name: Palmyra
properties.one_line: Palmyra sat squarely on the desert route silk had to cross to reach the Mediterranean, and its merchants grew rich charging for the privilege. Tomb excavations turned up actual fragments of Han-dynasty Chinese silk alongside silk thread meant for local reweaving. From this caravan city, cloth moved onward to the dye works of Tyre, Sidon, and Antioch. Palmyrene traders called their oasis home the 'Venice of the Sands.'
properties.image_credit: Roman ruins, Palmyra, Syria · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Colonnaded ruins at Palmyra

properties.name: Petra
properties.one_line: Petra's rock-cut capital grew wealthy as a clearinghouse where Chinese silk, Indian spice, and Arabian incense all changed hands before heading to Gaza and the Mediterranean. Rome annexed the Nabataean kingdom in 106 CE, folding this caravan hub directly into its new province of Arabia. From here, camel trains split toward Damascus, Gaza, and the Red Sea. Long-distance trade through the city hit its peak in the decades right after annexation.
properties.image_credit: Al-Khazneh (The Treasury), Petra, Jordan, by Vyacheslav Argenberg · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: The Treasury facade at Petra

properties.name: Alexandria
properties.one_line: Alexandria was the Mediterranean's other silk door, the one reached by sea rather than camel. Cargo landed at Red Sea ports, crossed the desert by caravan to the Nile, and floated downriver into the city's warehouses. From there, ships carried Chinese and Indian silk on to Rome and the rest of the empire. The route made Alexandria one of the two great funnels through which Chinese silk entered the Roman economy.
properties.image_credit: Pompey's Pillar, Alexandria · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Pompey's Pillar in Alexandria, Egypt

properties.name: Kos
properties.one_line: Kos wove its own gauzy fabric from a wild Mediterranean moth, not imported Chinese silk, and Roman patricians loved it anyway. Aristotle described the process back in the 4th century BC; Pliny the Elder credited a Coan woman named Pamphila with discovering it. Weavers on the island unwound cocoons of Pachypasa otus, spinning them into cloth so thin it could be dyed vivid purple and striped with gold. Roman writers still spoke of vestes Coae, garments from Kos, into the early empire.
properties.image_credit: Ancient Agora of Kos · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Columns of the ancient agora on Kos

properties.name: Alexandria
properties.one_line: Alexandria's looms turned Egyptian flax into linen fine enough for aristocrats and coarse enough for everyday tunics, selling both across the empire. The city held onto its lead in light textile production straight through pharaonic, Greek, and Roman rule alike. Weavers combined a linen base with dyed wool bands called clavi to finish a standard Roman tunic. Markets from Rome to Athens stocked Alexandrian linen by the bolt.
properties.image_credit: Catacombs of Kom El Shoqafa, Alexandria, by Leon Petrosyan · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Catacombs of Kom El Shoqafa in Alexandria

properties.name: Akhmim
properties.one_line: Akhmim wove linen for so long that the geographer Strabo already called it an ancient industry in his own lifetime. Under its Greek name, Panopolis, the town supplied fine flax cloth from the pharaohs' era straight through Roman rule. Its cemeteries later preserved hundreds of tunics, hangings, and shrouds, giving Egyptology some of its richest surviving Roman-era textiles. Strabo named only two industries here: linen-weaving and stone-cutting.
properties.image_credit: Open-air museum at the Temple of Min, Akhmim · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Open-air museum at the Temple of Min in Akhmim

properties.name: Miletus
properties.one_line: Miletus grazed its flocks on wide upland pasture and turned the fleece into a wool so soft it became a byword for luxury across the ancient Mediterranean. Roman writers ranked Milesian wool alongside the finest that Attica or Tarentum could produce. Garments cut from it counted as a mark of refinement rather than mere warmth. The city's long-running textile trade helped keep it among Ionia's wealthiest ports well into the Roman period.
properties.image_credit: Agora of Miletus · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ruins of the agora at Miletus

properties.name: Taranto
properties.one_line: Tarentum bred sheep so prized for their fleece that shepherds dressed the animals in leather jackets just to keep the wool clean while grazing. Pliny the Elder singled the local breed out for its exceptionally fine, soft, pure-white fiber. Cloaks cut from Tarentine and Apulian wool set the standard the rest of Roman Italy's textile trade measured itself against. The city built a Mediterranean-facing wool economy on top of its famous harbor and fisheries.
properties.image_credit: Doric columns of the Temple of Poseidon, Taranto · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Doric columns of an ancient temple in Taranto

properties.name: Padua
properties.one_line: Patavium turned the wool from its surrounding hills into carpets and cloaks that traveled straight to Augustus-era Rome. The geographer Strabo called it the wealthiest city in northern Italy and counted no fewer than five hundred Roman knights among its citizens, wealth he traced directly to its wool trade. Textiles, not farmland alone, made the city rich. Rough cloaks and fine hangings both left Patavium's workshops for markets across Italy.
properties.image_credit: Roman Arena, Padua · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Remains of the Roman Arena in Padua

properties.name: Cordoba
properties.one_line: Corduba spun and exported the pale golden wool of Baetica, a fleece the poet Martial praised by name as a river gilded by its own sheep. Roman Spain shipped this wool alongside olive oil and garum as one of Baetica's signature exports. Andalusian flocks kept their yellow-toned wool while black wool dominated the rest of the peninsula, a distinction ancient writers noted specifically. Cordoba's position on the Guadalquivir made it a natural spinning and export point for the trade.
properties.image_credit: Roman Bridge, Cordoba, Andalucia, Spain · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman bridge over the Guadalquivir at Cordoba

properties.name: Aquileia
properties.one_line: Aquileia sat at the southern end of the Amber Road, the overland route that carried raw Baltic amber down the Vistula and over the Alps to the Adriatic. Workshops in the city cut and polished that raw material into jewelry, carved ornaments, and medicinal preparations sold across the empire. Archaeologists have found that unworked amber, not finished pieces, arrived here, meaning the carving itself happened locally. The trade helped make Aquileia one of the richest cities in Roman Italy.
properties.image_credit: Roman Forum, Aquileia · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Remains of the Roman forum at Aquileia

properties.name: Charax Spasinou
properties.one_line: Charax Spasinou sat at the head of the Persian Gulf and controlled the gateway through which Gulf pearls reached Roman buyers. Isidorus of Charax documented pearl fishing here in the 1st century BC, and Palmyrene merchants kept permanent trading posts in the city to move the catch onward. Local kings minted their own coinage for over three centuries, a run that speaks to the port's lasting wealth. Pliny the Elder later called the Gulf pearl fishery the most productive in the world.
properties.image_credit: Coin of Hyspaosines, minted at Charax Spasinu · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ancient coin minted at Charax Spasinu

properties.name: Farasan Islands
properties.one_line: The Farasan Islands guarded the strait leading to the Red Sea's richest pearl beds, near the Bab-el-Mandeb chokepoint Roman traders had to pass. A Roman garrison stationed here, recorded in Latin inscriptions cut into the rock, protected shipping lanes and nearby pearling grounds from pirates. Pliny the Elder, writing in the 70s CE, already described pearl fisheries working this stretch of the Red Sea. The islands doubled as a customs checkpoint for Indian Ocean trade passing beneath them.
properties.image_credit: Farasan Island · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Coastline of Farasan Island, Saudi Arabia

properties.name: Conwy
properties.one_line: Conwy's river held freshwater pearl mussels that ancient writers linked to one of Rome's most famous jewels. Pliny the Elder reported that Julius Caesar dedicated a breastplate set with British pearls to Venus Genetrix in her Roman temple, and Suetonius names pearls among Caesar's reasons for eyeing Britain at all. Modern historians trace those pearls to the mussel beds around Conwy on the north Welsh coast. By the 16th century the same river still yielded up to 4 kilograms of pearls a week.
properties.image_credit: Conwy Castle, North Wales · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Conwy Castle on the river Conwy

properties.name: Paphos
properties.one_line: Paphos processed island flowers into scented oils at a scale that left presses, perfumery vessels, and residue for archaeologists to find. As Roman Cyprus's capital and the legendary birthplace of Aphrodite, the city tied its perfume trade to the goddess's own myth. Pliny the Elder, Theophrastus, and Dioscorides all wrote about Cypriot scent production in the same breath as its temples. Cyprus's rose-based perfumes carried a reputation across the Roman world for centuries.
properties.image_credit: House of Dionysus, Paphos Archaeological Park · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Mosaic floor at the House of Dionysus, Paphos

properties.name: Ein Gedi
properties.one_line: Ein Gedi grew the one plant Rome prized above every other scent: balsam, a resin Pliny the Elder said Judaea alone could produce. Growing it was a royal monopoly, and after 70 CE the emperor's treasury took it over, displaying a balsam bush in Vespasian and Titus's triumph through Rome. Jewish rebels reportedly tried burning the groves rather than let Rome seize them, while Roman troops fought to save the trees. By 117 CE the oasis supplied the empire's single most exclusive perfume ingredient.
properties.image_credit: Ein Gedi beach on the Dead Sea · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ein Gedi oasis on the shore of the Dead Sea

properties.name: Sidon
properties.one_line: Sidon gave the ancient world glassblowing itself, a technique its craftsmen developed around 50 BCE by inflating molten glass through a hollow tube. Pliny the Elder credited the city by name for the innovation he called flatu figurae, shaping by breath. The Sidonian glassmaker Ennion signed his own mold-blown jugs and cups in the 1st century CE, some of the earliest branded luxury goods in history. His work traveled and was copied as far away as Italy within his own lifetime.
properties.image_credit: Mold-blown glass jug signed by Ennion of Sidon, Metropolitan Museum of Art · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman mold-blown glass jug signed by Ennion

properties.name: Alexandria
properties.one_line: Alexandria's glassmakers perfected mosaic and millefiori techniques, fusing bundles of colored glass rods into canes that revealed flower-like patterns when sliced crosswise. The city had already led the Mediterranean in specialized glass techniques since the 1st century BCE, and one Roman writer described its finest pieces as nearly indistinguishable from rock crystal. Alexandrian glass traveled to Italy and beyond as some of the most prized tableware in the Roman world.
properties.image_credit: Pompey's Pillar, Alexandria · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Pompey's Pillar in Alexandria

properties.name: Pozzuoli
properties.one_line: Puteoli turned Campania's coastal sand into glassware, using the same littoral sand deposits Pliny the Elder named as a glassmaking source. Workshops around the Bay of Naples remelted imported Levantine raw glass alongside local material to finish vessels close to the capital. Its harbor, already Italy's busiest commercial port, made it a natural secondary hub for luxury glass. Pliny's Natural History, published in 77 CE, is the best-surviving ancient account of how that glass was made.
properties.image_credit: Macellum of Pozzuoli (Temple of Serapis) · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ruins of the Macellum of Pozzuoli

properties.name: Cologne
properties.one_line: Cologne began making glass almost as soon as Rome founded it as a colony in 50 CE, with 1st-century pieces already turning up beneath the modern city. Its industry expanded through the Flavian and Trajanic decades but only reached its real peak in the 2nd and 3rd centuries, producing the elaborate cage cups it's now famous for. At 117 CE the workshops were still young and growing, not yet the mature industry they later became.
properties.image_credit: Romisch-Germanisches Museum, Cologne · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Romano-Germanic Museum in Cologne

properties.name: Corinth
properties.one_line: Corinth once produced a bronze alloy so prized that Pliny the Elder ranked it above silver, mixed with gold and silver for a shimmer no other metalwork could match. Rome's sack of the city in 146 BCE scattered its workshops and killed off the artisans who knew the formula, and within a generation the alloy could no longer be reliably made. By Pliny's own day, genuine Corinthian bronze was already a rarity chased by collectors, with fakes far more common than the real thing.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Apollo, Corinth · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Doric columns of the Temple of Apollo at Corinth

properties.name: Capua
properties.one_line: Capua ranked as the second city of Italy in wealth, built in large part on bronze vases and vessels its workshops had turned out since at least the 6th century BCE. Both Cato the Elder and Pliny the Elder praised the city's bronzework by name. Etruscan metalworking know-how, absorbed early in Capua's history, kept its foundries running through Samnite, Roman, and imperial rule alike. Its amphitheater, the second-largest in the Roman world, still stands as a monument to that trade wealth.
properties.image_credit: Amphitheatre of Santa Maria Capua Vetere · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman amphitheatre at Santa Maria Capua Vetere

properties.name: Aegina
properties.one_line: Aegina's bronze once rivaled Corinth's for prestige, with Pliny the Elder ranking Aeginetan alloy among the finest the ancient world produced. That fame belonged mostly to the island's Classical and Hellenistic heyday, not a thriving Roman-period workshop. By 117 CE Aegina had long faded from its old naval and commercial power, eclipsed by Athens and folded quietly into Roman Achaea. It kept minting its own bronze coinage, a faint echo of a fame that was by then mostly historical.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Aphaia, Aegina · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Temple of Aphaia on the island of Aegina

properties.name: Alexandria
properties.one_line: Alexandria ranked alongside Rome and Antioch as one of the empire's three great centers for fine goldsmithing. Its workshops built on Hellenistic Egyptian techniques, setting gold jewelry with garnets and emeralds mined from Egypt's own eastern desert. The city's location made it the natural place where Egyptian gold, Nubian imports, and Greek design sense all met on the same workbench. Alexandrian goldwork traveled the Mediterranean as a mark of Roman-Egyptian luxury.
properties.image_credit: Pompey's Pillar with sphinx, Alexandria · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Pompey's Pillar and a sphinx statue in Alexandria

properties.name: Antioch
properties.one_line: Antioch stood beside Rome and Alexandria as one of the empire's three main jewelry centers, fed by wealthy Syria around it. Goldsmiths worked gold, gemstones, and glass into pieces sold across the eastern Mediterranean. As Syria's capital and one of the empire's largest cities, Antioch had the wealth and trade links to run goldsmithing at real scale. A dining-room mosaic made there around 115-150 CE, now in the Louvre, shows the craftsmanship its workshops produced in this exact period.
properties.image_credit: Mosaic of the Judgment of Paris, from Antioch, Louvre Museum · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman mosaic from Antioch depicting the Judgment of Paris

properties.name: Kythira
properties.one_line: Kythira's ancient name, Porphyroussa, meant simply ‘the purple island’ — a name that stuck for a shoreline littered with crushed murex shell. Fishermen worked the same banded dye-murex prized at Tyre and Sidon, hauling snails from rocky coves for more than a thousand years. The island's remote position between Crete and the Peloponnese made this small outpost surprisingly rich. Archaeologists have traced the dye works back to the Bronze Age, still running when Rome ruled the Aegean.
properties.image_credit: Cythera Capital and the Castle · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: View of Chora, the capital of Kythira, and its castle

properties.name: Essaouira
properties.one_line: Client king Juba II built a purple-dye factory on the islets off Mogador around 25 BCE, turning this Atlantic coastline into a dye-producing outpost far beyond the Mediterranean core. Workers crushed murex and purpura shells gathered from tidal rocks between the islands and the mainland. The operation ran for roughly three centuries, supplying the purple stripe worn on Roman senatorial togas. Pliny the Elder listed the site by name among the empire's dye sources.
properties.image_credit: Ramparts of Essaouira, near the ancient Purple Islands · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ramparts of Essaouira on Morocco's Atlantic coast

properties.name: Cadiz
properties.one_line: Cadiz was already dyeing purple from murex trunculus by 800 BCE, when Phoenician settlers built a shellfish-crushing kiln unearthed beneath the city's old Teatro Cómico. That shellstone-lined workshop is the earliest known purple-dye facility on Europe's Atlantic coast. Roman-era Gades kept the trade running, drawing on the same beds just outside the Pillars of Hercules. Its harbor, already the empire's gateway to Atlantic Iberia, doubled as an outlet for the pigment.
properties.image_credit: Roman Theatre of Cadiz · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Seating tiers of the Roman theatre at Cadiz

properties.name: Taranto
properties.one_line: Tarentum ran a purple-dye industry so large that mounds of crushed murex shell still rise along the Mare Piccolo lagoon shore. Pliny the Elder ranked Tarentine purple second only to Tyrian, once the most fashionable dye money could buy in Rome. Workshops crushed shellfish hauled from the lagoon's sheltered waters, later famous for oyster farming instead. Tyrian dibapha, selling for some 1,000 denarii a pound, eventually eclipsed it, but Tarentine dye works kept running regardless.
properties.image_credit: Doric columns of the Temple of Poseidon, Taranto · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Doric columns of an ancient temple in Taranto

properties.name: Laodicea
properties.one_line: Laodicea grew rich on wool so black and glossy that Strabo credited the fertility of its pastures for the color. Local flocks produced a raven-black fleece unlike anything else in Asia Minor, woven into garments called trimita and sold across the Roman world. The wealth it brought made the city a byword for self-satisfied prosperity. Two rival textile towns, Hierapolis and Colossae, sat within 12 miles, making the Lycus valley one dense cluster of Roman wool production.
properties.image_credit: Western Theatre, Laodicea on the Lycus · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ruins of the western theatre at Laodicea on the Lycus

properties.name: Colossae
properties.one_line: Colossae lent its own name to a color: colossinus, a dark reddish-purple wool dye Pliny the Elder compared to a cyclamen flower. The city's wool was dyed on-site into this signature hue and exported as a recognizable brand across the Roman world. Colossae sat in the Lycus valley beside two rival wool towns, Laodicea and Hierapolis, each with its own specialty color. By 117 CE it had already begun losing ground to its larger neighbor, though its dye still carried its own name.
properties.image_credit: Colossae archaeological site · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: The mound of ancient Colossae in the Lycus valley

properties.name: Cirencester
properties.one_line: Corinium grew into Roman Britain's second-largest town partly on its wool trade, with nearby graves yielding wool combs marking out wealthy merchants. Villas around the settlement ran sheep across the same grassland that later built the medieval Cotswold wool fortunes. As capital of the Dobunni tribe's new civitas, the town collected taxes partly in raw fleece. Britain's hooded wool cloaks, prized enough for their own listing in a later price edict, had roots in pastures like these.
properties.image_credit: Cirencester Roman Amphitheatre · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Grassy earthworks of the Roman amphitheatre at Cirencester

properties.name: Canosa di Puglia
properties.one_line: Canusium turned its tawny-brown fleece into a wool so recognizable that Pliny the Elder named the color after the town itself. Garments cut from it, called canusinae, were prized for their durability as much as their warmth. The city sat close enough to Tarentum's famous flocks that Roman writers ranked the two wool centers together as Apulia's finest. Canusium later added a triumphal arch, raised around 109 CE under Trajan, a mark of the wealth its wool trade helped build.
properties.image_credit: Arch of Trajan, Canosa di Puglia · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: The Roman Arch of Trajan at Canosa di Puglia

properties.name: Merv
properties.one_line: Merv sat where every branch of the Silk Road converged before splitting toward Parthia, Mesopotamia, and eventually Rome. Han Chinese silk crossed this Central Asian oasis on its way west, changing hands long before it touched ports like Palmyra or Alexandria. Canals fed by the Murghab River made the oasis rich enough to be called the largest city on the route. Alexander the Great founded a city here four centuries earlier; by 117 CE it thrived as a Parthian hub beyond Rome's frontier.
properties.image_credit: Great Kyz Kala, ancient Merv · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: The ruined fortress of Great Kyz Kala at Merv

properties.name: Dura-Europos
properties.one_line: Dura-Europos perched above the Euphrates at the junction of the river route and the great east-west caravan road, a natural stop for silk moving toward Roman Syria. Palmyrene merchants kept a permanent presence in the city from at least 33 BCE, using it as a forward post for the caravan trade they dominated. Deep ravines flanking two sides made it easy to defend and hard to bypass. Later called the 'Pompeii of the Syrian desert,' it preserved its warehouses in remarkable detail under the sand.
properties.image_credit: Dura-Europos overlooking the Euphrates · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: The ruins of Dura-Europos above the Euphrates river

properties.name: Damascus
properties.one_line: Damascus became the spot where Asia's silk caravans handed their cargo to Mediterranean-bound traders, the place East and West did business face to face. Rome had governed it since Pompey annexed it in 64 BCE, and by Trajan's day its temple to Jupiter was redesigned by Apollodorus of Damascus, the same architect who later raised Trajan's Forum in Rome. Caravans loaded with silk, Indian spice, and Arabian perfume passed through toward the sea, a pattern that outlasted Roman rule by centuries.
properties.image_credit: Umayyad Mosque, built over the Roman Temple of Jupiter, Damascus · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: The Umayyad Mosque in Damascus, site of the Roman Temple of Jupiter

properties.name: Beit Shean
properties.one_line: Scythopolis wove linen so fine that the Jerusalem Talmud singled it out by name as a source of prized fabric. Jewish weavers dominated the trade, and Diocletian's price edict later ranked the city's textiles in its top quality class. As the only Decapolis city west of the Jordan River, Scythopolis paired a Greek civic identity with a workforce famous for weaving. Its Roman theater, built to seat roughly 7,000 spectators, still measures how much wealth that linen trade brought.
properties.image_credit: Roman theatre at Beit Shean (Scythopolis) · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: The Roman theatre at Beit Shean

properties.name: Muharraq
properties.one_line: Tylos, the ancient name for the island now called Bahrain, produced pearls Pliny the Elder ranked as the finest from the Persian Gulf. Isidore of Charax described divers working these waters a century before Pliny wrote, plunging from rafts to depths of twenty fathoms. The island's oyster beds fed a gulf-wide pearl trade that funneled outward through ports like Charax Spasinou toward Roman buyers. Divers here worked the same beds their descendants still harvested into the 20th century.

properties.name: Amathus
properties.one_line: Amathus burned incense and pressed scented oils at its temple of Aphrodite so long that censers there show unbroken use into the Byzantine period. As one of Cyprus's oldest royal cities, ruled independently for over a thousand years before Rome absorbed the island, it tied perfume-making to Aphrodite's own birthplace. Craftsmen used an olive-oil base infused with oak moss, bergamot, and labdanum resin from rockrose flowers. Its own harbor let scented oils leave Cyprus without routing through Paphos.
properties.image_credit: The Amathus sarcophagus, Metropolitan Museum of Art · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Painted limestone sarcophagus from Amathus, Cyprus

properties.name: Capua
properties.one_line: Capua ran an entire marketplace, the Seplasia, dedicated to nothing but perfumes and unguents. Campania's fields grew roses so abundantly that its rose oil, Rhodinum italicum, eclipsed the older Rhodinon once favored from Phaselis in Lycia. Pliny the Elder praised Capuan roses by name, ranking Campania's perfume trade second only to Egypt's. The city's wealth from wine and unguents made it Italy's second city by reputation, even after Rome punished it in 211 BCE for siding with Hannibal.
properties.image_credit: Amphitheatre of Santa Maria Capua Vetere · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman amphitheatre at Santa Maria Capua Vetere

properties.name: Beirut
properties.one_line: Berytus ran one of the Mediterranean's earliest glass furnaces, a production site excavated beneath the modern city and dated to the mid-1st century CE. Augustus had already refounded the city as a veterans' colony, funding the industries that grew up around it. Unlike centers that only reworked imported material, Berytus melted its own colored glass from scratch in purpose-built furnaces. Sidon may have invented glassblowing, but Berytus built its own furnaces to compete.
properties.image_credit: Roman Baths, Beirut · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Remains of the Roman baths in Beirut

properties.name: Aquileia
properties.one_line: Aquileia didn't just carve Baltic amber, it blew and cast glass on a serious scale too, leaving behind more than 6,000 carved glass gems in the city's museum. Workshops here remelted raw glass imported from the Levant and Egypt into finished vessels for northern Adriatic markets. Excavated melting-chamber fragments and tools confirm the furnaces ran through the 2nd and 3rd centuries. Aquileia sat at the head of the Amber Road and the top of the Adriatic, working two entirely different luxury materials.
properties.image_credit: Roman Forum, Aquileia · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Remains of the Roman forum at Aquileia

properties.name: Palestrina
properties.one_line: Praeneste turned out bronze cistae, cylindrical boxes engraved with mythological scenes, so refined that one surviving example, the Ficoroni Cista, names its own maker. Workshops paired these with pear-shaped bronze mirrors in a distinctive local style, neither fully Etruscan nor fully Roman. The craft peaked in the 4th and 3rd centuries BCE, well before Rome's empire took shape. By 117 CE the cista workshops were long silent, though the hill town still drew pilgrims to its huge Sanctuary of Fortuna.
properties.image_credit: Sanctuary of Fortuna Primigenia, Palestrina · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Terraced ramps of the Sanctuary of Fortuna Primigenia at Palestrina

properties.name: Orvieto
properties.one_line: Volsinii ran one of Etruria's biggest bronze industries, casting cookware and devotional statues in vast quantity. When Rome sacked the city in 264 BCE, its soldiers reportedly hauled off more than 2,000 bronze statues, melting many down into Roman coinage. The destruction was so total that the population was resettled near modern Bolsena, ending independent Etruscan rule for good. By 117 CE the old bronze-casting hilltop, now Orvieto, stood as a shadow of its former power.
properties.image_credit: Etruscan Temple of Belvedere, Orvieto · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Remains of the Etruscan Temple of Belvedere at Orvieto

properties.name: Sardis
properties.one_line: Sardis built its legendary wealth on gold panned from the Pactolus River, refined at a workshop that turned Lydian ore into the world's first true gold coinage under King Croesus. Archaeologists excavating Pactolus North uncovered the refinery itself, with the salt-cementation process used to purify the metal. That gold rush was already six centuries in the past by Trajan's reign, the river's placer deposits long since panned out. Sardis kept its reputation for riches anyway, 'rich as Croesus' outliving the mine.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Artemis, Sardis · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Columns of the Temple of Artemis at Sardis

properties.name: Petra
properties.one_line: Petra's Nabataean goldsmiths worked gold, silver, bronze, and iron into elaborate jewelry despite having no local source for precious metals — everything arrived by trade. Women here were buried wearing gold earrings and sometimes a gold nose ring, tied to piercing customs meant to ward off bad luck. Strabo remarked on how much silver and gold the Nabataeans held despite mining none of it. Rome's 106 CE annexation folded this goldworking tradition into the new province of Arabia.
